lead: Bulking is a planned phase of eating above maintenance calories, combined with resistance training, with the aim of gaining muscle and body weight. It is the counterpart of cutting, the phase in which body fat is reduced to reveal the muscle that has been built.[1] For people interested in appearance, bulking is the stage in which a broader, fuller frame is built: more shoulder, chest, arm and back mass, and the heavier body weight that supports it.

Bodybuilders traditionally bulk in the off-season and begin cutting roughly 12 to 14 weeks before a contest.[2] The length and size of the calorie surplus determines how much fat accompanies the muscle gained.[1] In looksmaxxing communities, bulking is discussed both as a route to physique and as a trade-off with facial and body leanness, and users on looksmax.org describe a wide range of experiences with it.[3][4]

Wikipedia states that the link between positive energy balance and muscle growth is the reason the bulk-and-cut cycle is considered effective, while noting that it is unclear how much lean mass is retained through a later cut.[1][2] Muscle physiology references likewise describe a positive energy balance as supporting anabolism over the long term, alongside mechanical tension from training, adequate protein and progressive overload.[5]

angle.text: Bulking supplies the energy that lets lifting turn into added muscle, which people use to build a broader upper body and heavier frame. Practitioners then cut to show the result, and communities discuss how large a surplus balances muscle gain against fat gain.

infobox: Off-season; cut begins about 12-14 weeks before a contest[2]

paras: Bulking means maintaining a calorie surplus to support muscle growth; the size of the surplus depends on goals, and a larger surplus or longer bulk adds more fat alongside muscle.[1]

Clean bulking (also called lean bulking) aims to add muscle with little fat. It is slower and relies on hitting calorie and macronutrient goals every day, commonly with moderate carbohydrate, moderate protein and low fat, and sometimes alternating higher- and lower-calorie days.[2] Dirty bulking uses a large surplus without precise tracking, often built on calorie-dense or junk food. It can add size and strength quickly but usually adds considerable body fat, which then requires a harsher cut.[2]

Grokipedia gives clean-bulk surpluses of roughly 250 to 500 kcal above maintenance and traces the practice to strongman culture, Eugen Sandow and the Weider brothers, though this source is AI-generated and not independently verified.[6]

Bodybuilders generally need more calories than an average person of the same weight. Protein recommendations in the bodybuilding literature vary: Wikipedia notes that 25 to 30 percent of calories from protein is commonly recommended, that some advocate about 1 gram per pound of bodyweight and others suggest less or more, and that protein is typically spread through the day and around training.[2] Muscle hypertrophy references cite a 2018 review recommending a minimum of about 1.6 g/kg/day for building lean tissue, with no additional hypertrophy seen above about 1.8 g/kg, while bodybuilders often advise higher figures.[5]

Carbohydrates are used to fuel training and, through insulin, to support protein synthesis; many lifters add fast carbohydrate sources such as dextrose or maltodextrin around workouts.[2] Creatine monohydrate and pre-workout products are other commonly used supplements; the usual creatine amounts described are 3 to 5 grams per day, and pre-workouts containing caffeine can impair sleep.[2]

Hypertrophy is mainly growth in the size of existing muscle cells rather than an increase in their number.[5] Mechanical tension from resistance training is the accepted though not fully settled driver, activating mTOR signaling and raising muscle protein synthesis, which can remain elevated for roughly 28 to 72 hours after a session depending on the study.[5] Frequency, intensity and total volume directly affect the result, and progressive increases in these produce growth.[5] A calorie surplus provides the energy and building material for this tissue to be added without being drawn from other uses.[1][5]
Genetics also shape response. A twin study cited on Wikipedia estimated about 53 percent heritability for lean body mass, and men gain muscle more easily than women because of testosterone.[5]

No studies found on bulking as a looksmaxxing practice. Related research on energy surplus, protein intake and muscle growth exists in the resistance-training literature and is summarised in general references on hypertrophy.[5]

A 2020 narrative review of nutrition for physique athletes (Roberts, Helms, Trexler and Fitschen) is the main review covering the competitive off-season. It does not prescribe a specific surplus or weekly gain rate, but reports off-season male bodybuilders eating about 3,800 kcal per day, warns that a very large surplus (a 40 percent overfeeding example) may cause substantial fat accretion, and recommends 1.8 to 2.7 g/kg/day of protein for physique athletes.[8] It also notes that the meta-analytic mean protein intake for maximising fat-free mass gain with resistance training is about 1.6 g/kg/day, with an upper confidence limit of 2.2 g/kg/day.[8]

sections.h: After the contest: regain and the off-season
paras: The same review describes the transition from contest prep back to the off-season as a period of rapid regain: some competitors regained up to 8 kg within three to four weeks, early regain is characterised by preferential fat gain, and the authors cite a risk of body fat overshooting prior levels.[8] They suggest a tapered but intentional surplus aiming to reach a sustainable body weight within one to two months, with intake guided by hunger and satiety cues and by feedback such as rate of weight gain rather than strict tracking.[8] Full physiological recovery is described as typically taking four to six months.[8]
For women, the review recommends an off-season intake of at least 30 kcal per kg of lean mass per day to protect menstrual function.[8]

Eugen Sandow staged an early bodybuilding contest, the Great Competition, at London's Royal Albert Hall on 14 September 1901.[2] Joe and Ben Weider founded the IFBB in 1946, and in the 1950s and 1960s magazines spread advice on bulking and cutting phases, protein and food supplements alongside the sport.[2] The off-season bulk followed by a pre-contest cut became the standard competitive cycle, and the vocabulary of clean and dirty bulking passed from bodybuilding into general gym and online fitness culture.[2]

Wikipedia lists excess fat gain, a harder cut and, over time, possible effects on cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity as risks of dirty bulking, and notes that anabolic steroid use, sometimes combined with bulking, carries serious risks.[1][2]

Users on looksmax.org describe bulking after a long cut as a relief: one poster who lost 20 kg over six months writes that moving from a 500 kcal deficit to a 250 kcal surplus meant 750 kcal more food and hours less cardio.[3] Other users argue that bulking worsens facial appearance, describing bloating, acne and a long cut afterwards.[4] A further thread argues that natural lifters do not need a surplus beyond the first year of training or when underweight, and that small surpluses are enough.[7] Replies in that thread recommend a clean bulk of about 250 kcal.[7]
The debate frames bulking as a trade-off between size and leanness, and it often appears together with discussion of when to stop a bulk and begin cutting, and of body recomposition.

On T Nation, bulking appears in training logs and challenges. Members describe a conservative surplus of about 300 calories of carbohydrate as the conventional approach, which one poster says suits some natural lifters but is the exception rather than the rule;[9] others describe dirty bulks with calorie-dense meals,[10] bulks that were not completely dirty,[11] or extended bulks ending in a dirty phase for a transformation challenge.[12] A further group says it follows a no-bulk, no-cut philosophy of training at maintenance.[13] The related practices of lean bulking and dirty bulking have their own article on this wiki.

lore.intro: Bulking is discussed on looksmax.org as a way to build size, as a relief after cutting, and as a trade-off with leanness and facial appearance.[3][4][7]

claims.claim: A calorie surplus is the way to gain muscle.
claims.believers: Proponents describe moving from a deficit to a small surplus as freeing and as supporting growth.[3]
claims.experts: Wikipedia states that the link between positive energy balance and muscle growth is the reason the cycle is considered effective.[1]

claims.claim: Natural lifters do not need to bulk beyond early training.
claims.believers: One user argues natural lifters can gain the same muscle on maintenance or a deficit, only slower, and that surplus calories mostly add fat except for beginners or the underweight.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia notes it is unclear how much muscle is retained through cutting and whether the process is worthwhile overall.[1]

claims.claim: A small surplus of about 250 calories gives minimal fat gain.
claims.believers: A reply in the thread recommends a "clean bulk" at that surplus.[7]
claims.experts: Wikipedia describes clean bulking as slower with little fat gain, while a larger surplus or longer bulk adds more fat.[1][2]

claims.believers: One poster says a bulk left them bloated and acne-prone and that it took months of restricting to return to a preferred weight.[4]
claims.experts: No published studies have examined facial appearance across bulking phases; Wikipedia describes fat gain as an expected result of a surplus.[1]

name: Bulking

card.summary: Eat above maintenance to build muscle; the debate is how much fat comes along.
card.note: Dirty bulks add more fat; steroid use alongside bulking carries separate serious risks.

quick.overview:
Bulking is eating in a calorie surplus alongside lifting to gain muscle. Clean bulks use a small surplus; dirty bulks use a large one.

The energy-balance link to muscle growth is well established, but forum users debate whether natural lifters need it and how much fat it adds.
quick.mechanism: Surplus calories and protein provide energy and material for muscle growth under progressive resistance training.
quick.risks: Larger surpluses add more body fat and may require a longer cut; dirty bulking may affect cholesterol and insulin sensitivity over time.
